children.text: New Census Bureau figures revealed that more than 36 million Americans were living in poverty, with Latino/as bearing a disproportionate share of the burden. Twenty-nine out of every 100 Latino/as were counted as poor, and more than half of Hispanic children fell below the poverty line. Black and Hispanic Americans were roughly three times more likely to be poor than white Americans. The data also showed that poor Latino/as were less likely to have health insurance than other groups.
New York City Puerto Rican Plebiscite

Puerto Ricans in New York City held their own non-binding vote on the island's political status, parallel to the November plebiscite planned for Puerto Rico itself. Voters could choose statehood, continued commonwealth status, or independence. Organizers argued that Puerto Ricans living on the mainland, many of whom vote in U.S. elections, deserved a voice in the debate. Coalition leader Manny Mirabal pointed out that 143 members of Congress represent districts with significant Puerto Rican populations, and that the New York results could pressure those representatives to take up the status question more seriously.

Members of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus introduced legislation to increase funding for the National Center on Health Statistics, whose data shapes how federal healthcare dollars are distributed. Congresswoman Lucille Roybal-Allard emphasized that Latinas face higher rates of diabetes and other diseases compared to other groups of women, and that better data collection was essential to addressing those disparities. Caucus members framed the bill as complementary to, not competing with, the Clinton administration's broader healthcare reform effort.
Environmental Justice Coalition Meets in Washington

For the first time, leaders of the nation's environmental justice movement, representing African American, Asian American, Native American, and Latino/a organizations, gathered together in Washington. Richard Moore of the Southwest Network for Environmental and Economic Justice in Albuquerque explained that Latino/a communities had long been engaged in environmental struggles without always naming them as such. Farmworker pesticide campaigns, lead paint in housing projects, and the placement of industrial facilities next to low-income Latino/a neighborhoods were all cited as examples of environmental injustice that predated the formal movement.
Operation Blockade and the El Paso Economy

Now in its third week, Operation Blockade, the Border Patrol's intensive enforcement along a 20-mile stretch of the U.S.-Mexico border at El Paso, was taking a severe toll on downtown merchants. Business was down as much as 90 percent for some shop owners, many of whom depended on shoppers crossing legally from Ciudad Juárez. Confusion and fear about the operation led even legal crossers to stay away. Community leaders and tourism officials on both sides of the border called for dialogue, emphasizing the deep economic interdependence of El Paso and Juarez. Border Patrol Chief Sylvester Reyes said illegal-crossing arrests had fallen by 80 percent and that the operation would continue indefinitely.
Congressional Hispanic Caucus Electronic Town Hall

Nearly 800 invited guests and all 20 members of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus participated in a seven-city electronic town hall linking San Juan, Miami, New York, Chicago, Los Angeles, San Antonio, and Washington. The event was the culmination of a three-day issues forum on Capitol Hill. A survey of participants ranked education as the top concern, followed by health, community viability, and the environment. Questions from the audience touched on bilingual education, the anti-immigrant climate, and the exclusion of undocumented people from the administration's healthcare proposal. Illinois Congressman Luis Gutierrez argued that healthcare should be treated as a fundamental human right regardless of immigration status. Caucus chair Jose Serrano reaffirmed that the caucus viewed undocumented immigrants as part of the community it serves. Secretary Henry Cisneros opened by urging unity across the caucus's diverse membership. The group also demonstrated new political muscle by blocking a bill that would have extended unemployment insurance by cutting benefits for blind and disabled legal immigrants. Congressman Xavier Becerra's closing message to the audience: vote, vote, vote.

The MTV cable network launched MTV Latino, a 24-hour Spanish-language music network distributed across 11 Latin American countries and select U.S. cities including Miami, Tucson, Boston, Fresno, and Sacramento. Miami had become the undisputed hub of the U.S. Latin entertainment industry, home to Sony Discos, Telemundo, Univision, and dozens of Spanish-language radio stations and print outlets. Nearly 60 percent of Miami's population was Hispanic, and the city's proximity and transportation links to Latin America made it an ideal headquarters. Sony Discos vice president Angel Carrasco predicted a growing crossover between Latin and mainstream Anglo markets, citing Gloria Estefan as a model. The MTV Latino launch party on Miami's South Beach drew hundreds of guests, with host Daisy Fuentes serving as master of ceremonies. Despite the Spanish-language branding, over three-quarters of the music on the new network was expected to come from Anglo artists, reflecting, according to MTV executives, what Latin American teens wanted to hear.
